title: Equivalence Relations, Classes and Partitions
quickIdea: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and it is the same object as a partition of the set. Counting equivalence relations is counting partitions, which is the Bell number.
remember: An equivalence relation is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
The equivalence class of a is the set of all elements related to a; classes are non-empty and any two are either identical or disjoint.
The classes of an equivalence relation partition the set: every element lies in exactly one class.
Conversely, every partition of A defines exactly one equivalence relation, namely 'lies in the same block'. So equivalence relations on A and partitions of A are in bijection.
The number of equivalence relations on an n-element set is the Bell number B(n): 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52 for n = 0 to 5.
The number with exactly k classes is the Stirling number of the second kind S(n, k), and the Bell number is the sum of S(n, k) over k.
Congruence modulo m on the integers is the standard example: the classes are the m residue classes.
Refining a partition means splitting blocks, and the corresponding equivalence relations are nested; this is how GATE phrases questions about refinement.
The union of two equivalence relations is generally not an equivalence relation, but their intersection always is.

example.prompt: A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. How many equivalence relations are there, and how many have exactly two classes?
example.work: Count the partitions by block sizes: 4 gives 1; 3+1 gives 4; 2+2 gives 3; 2+1+1 gives 6; 1+1+1+1 gives 1. The total is 15, which is B(4). Two-class partitions are the 3+1 and 2+2 shapes, so 4 + 3 = 7, which is S(4, 2).
example.answer: 15 equivalence relations, of which 7 have exactly two classes.

gateAngle: GATE CS 1997 Q.6.3 asks for the number of equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3, 4} and the options include 15, which is the Bell number B(4) built from the five partition shapes.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: See GATE CS 1997 Q.6.3 in the linked PYQs.
variations.why: Equivalence relations correspond to partitions, and {1,2,3,4} has 1 + 4 + 3 + 6 + 1 = 15 partitions.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is the union of two equivalence relations on the same set always an equivalence relation?
variations.answer: No. The intersection always is; the union need not be.
variations.why: Take the partitions {{1,2},{3}} and {{1},{2,3}}. The union of the two relations contains (1,2) and (2,3) but not (1,3), so it is not transitive.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: How many equivalence relations on a 3-element set have exactly two classes?
variations.why: The two-class shapes are 2+1, and choosing the block of size 2 from 3 elements gives C(3,2) = 3. The Bell number 5 splits as 1 (one class) + 3 (two classes) + 1 (three classes).

trap.what: Forgetting that the classes must cover the whole set, or treating a symmetric transitive relation as an equivalence relation without checking the diagonal.
trap.why: A partition has no empty block and no missing element. A relation that is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive leaves elements outside every class, so it corresponds to a partition of a proper subset, not of the set.
trap.counterexample: A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1,2), (2,1), (1,1), (2,2)}. Symmetric and transitive, but 3 is related to nothing, not even itself, so the 'classes' {1, 2} and nothing for 3 do not partition A.

check.question: How many partitions does a 3-element set have, and what is the equivalence relation with the fewest classes?
check.answer: 5 partitions; the relation with one class is the universal relation A x A.
check.explanation: The shapes are 3, 2+1 (three of them) and 1+1+1, giving 1 + 3 + 1 = 5. One class means every pair is related, which is the whole product.
